extraction.title: Why Is There So Little Money in U.S. Politics?
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (1836 lines) in three chunks, all body sections, Tables 1-4 and endnotes. Figures 1A and 1B read from axis labels and prose only. Page numbers are printed NBER pages from the extraction, may be off by one. Annotations: annot_sha12s empty, n_annots 0, no _annots file read; paul_markup empty (0 items, 0 dropped). No note flag, so not a Paul note. Metadata hints checked and correct; no DOI in text. No networks, path-finding, persuasion/turnout or text measurement in paper. Key findings capped at 12.
extraction.research_question: Why is there so little money in U.S. politics given the large value of policies at stake (Tullock 1972 puzzle), and why do organized interests give at all? The authors argue that campaign giving is mainly consumption and participation by individuals, not investment in legislation.
extraction.theory: Campaign contributions as investments in a political market for private benefits (Snyder 1990; Grossman and Helpman 1994; Denzau and Munger 1986; monopoly-donor models of Dal-Bo 2001 and Helpman and Persson 2001) versus contributions as consumption of participation, like charitable giving (consumer contributors who are ideologically motivated, asked by friends, and civically active). For interest groups the authors list four or five possible reasons for giving: small return, buying access, electing friends, coordinating individual donors, and consumption by executives.
extraction.data: (a) Survey of nearly 40 roll-call studies (Table 1). (b) Chamber of Commerce roll-call score, U.S. House 1978-1994, N = 3400 (Table 2). (c) FEC-era totals 1978-2000 and presidential spending 1884-2000 (Figure 1). (d) Gubernatorial state panel 1976-2000, N = 326 (Table 3), with BEA income and Census finance data. (e) House elections 1992-2000 with district income and margins (Table 4, 1735 races) and Senate spending by state size. (f) 94 executives at 12 large firms, 1997-98 cycle (ExecuComp, Center for Responsive Politics). (g) 2000 totals from FEC and PAC accounts; 2000 ANES survey.
extraction.method: Descriptive accounting of contributions by source; tabulation of prior roll-call studies by significance and sign; OLS and two-stage IV regressions of the CCUS score on corporate and labor PAC money with year effects and either party plus district preference, district fixed effects, or member fixed effects; OLS state fixed-effects panel of log per-capita gubernatorial spending; cross-section regressions of House race spending on district income and margin with year, party and incumbency controls; time-series ratios of spending to GDP and national income.
extraction.identification: IV for PAC money using electoral competition (opponent spending, absolute vote share minus .5, unopposed dummy) and member power (party leader, committee chair, Ways and Means or Energy and Commerce membership), following Chappell 1982 and Welch 1982. Member fixed effects absorb time-invariant member preferences. Gubernatorial estimates rely on within-state variation with state fixed effects. Time-series, executive and aggregate-share results are descriptive with no causal identification.
extraction.measures: CCUS roll-call score 0-100 per member-year; corporate and labor PAC contributions in dollars; member party; district partisanship; per-capita personal income; per-capita state and federal government spending; population; closeness of general and primary elections (1 minus winner vote share); total campaign spending by all candidates; spending as a share of GDP or national income.
extraction.scope: U.S. federal (House, Senate, president) and state (governor) elections under FECA, mainly 1976-2000; presidential spending 1884-2000; roll-call evidence for the U.S. House 1978-1994; PAC activity in 2000; executives in the 1997-98 cycle. Units are contributors (individuals, PACs, firms), legislators and states. Claims about the whole system are broad, drawn from these pieces.
key_findings: Individuals gave nearly 2.4 billion of about 3 billion dollars in 1999-2000; about 21 million people (about 10 percent of adults) gave, averaging about 115 dollars (p.7).
Only 4 percent of PAC contributions to House and Senate candidates are at or near the 10000 dollar limit; the average PAC gift is 1700 dollars and the modal contribution is zero (p.8).

In 2000 PACs spent 579.4 million dollars in total; 280.8 million went to or for candidates and about 300 million to overhead and other activity that could have been paid by the sponsor's treasury (p.9).
In a survey of nearly 40 roll-call studies, PAC contributions had no significant effect or the wrong sign in three of four instances (Table 1, p.15).

CCUS model, House 1978-1994, N = 3400: an extra 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money (about one SD) moves the 0-100 score by at most 2 points, while a change of party moves it more than 30 points (pp.18-19).
District fixed effects nearly eliminate the contribution effects, and member fixed effects eliminate them entirely; coefficients are tiny and insignificant in OLS and IV (Table 2, p.19).

IV estimates shrink the effects and reverse the sign on corporate money (column 4 coefficient -0.30, Table 2); the authors conclude the evidence for substantial vote influence is rather thin (pp.19-20).
Interest groups spent about 3 billion dollars on lobbying in 1997-98, roughly ten times the 300 million they spent on PAC contributions (p.32, citing Ansolabehere Snyder and Tripathi 2002).

Tullock puzzle restated: 2000 campaign spending was about 3 billion dollars against 2 trillion of federal spending; 192000 dollars of 1985 sugar-industry contributions preceded a subsidy vote, with the subsidy worth over 5 billion dollars over five years (pp.11-13).

Executives: 94 top executives at 12 firms gave about 7500 dollars per cycle, or 51 dollars per 100000 of income (0.05 percent), close to the 0.04 percent of national income spent on campaigns in 2000 (p.22).

Real campaign spending roughly doubled 1976-2000 but has no trend relative to national income; presidential spending as a share of GDP was flat 1912-2000 and about three times higher in the 1880s and 1890s (pp.23-24).

Gubernatorial panel 1976-2000 (N = 326, state fixed effects): income elasticity about 1.07 to 1.17, government spending has no independent effect (-0.09), and closeness has a strong positive effect (2.93) (Table 3, pp.26-27). House races 1992-2000: each 1000 dollars of district income adds about 20000 dollars of spending; close races attract 60 percent of money from individuals versus 31 percent from PACs (pp.28-29).
limitations: Literature magnitudes are hard to compare because most studies do not report means or standard deviations (p.16).
Simultaneity between contributions and votes, and omitted district and donor-strength controls, may bias the roll-call estimates (pp.16-17).
The IV results are sensitive to instrument choice; sign and size change across specifications (p.19).
The consumption account lacks specific empirical predictions that separate it from rent-seeking; the authors say the theory is undeveloped (p.31).
The party coefficient may partly reflect party money or interest-group money routed through parties (endnote 9, p.58).

Party account transfers may double count about 10 percent of party money; the 380 million soft-money figure is estimated from FEC individual donor files; industry totals are called overestimates (endnotes 3-5).
The House regression is reported only in text, with a linear statement (20000 dollars per 1000) and a log footnote (elasticity 0.43) that are not reconciled (p.28, endnote 12).

Table 2 extraction is garbled; one labor IV cell is starred significant in the extraction while the text calls legislator-FE effects insignificant, and the text's 6-point labor effect has no matching positive coefficient.
Executive sample is 94 people at 12 firms; state data are limited to 1976-2000; the presidential series is of lower data quality by the authors' own account (p.22).
The 20 percent return on investment for a subset of PACs is an illustration, not an estimate (p.32).
short_quotes: campaign contributions are not a form of policy-buying, but are rather a form of political participation and consumption
the question is not why there is so little money politics, but rather why organized interests give at all
Money has little leverage because it is only a small part of the political calculation that a reelection oriented legislator makes

summary_md: Ansolabehere, de Figueiredo and Snyder (NBER WP 9409, 2002) restate the Tullock puzzle. In 2000 about 3 billion dollars went to campaigns, against 2 trillion of federal spending. They answer that campaign money is mostly individual consumption and participation, not policy purchase. Individuals gave about 2.4 of the 3 billion dollars. Only 4 percent of PAC gifts are near the limit. In nearly 40 roll-call studies, PAC effects are null or wrongly signed three times in four. In their own House panel (1978-1994, N = 3400), 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money moves a 0-100 Chamber score by at most 2 points, while party moves it by more than 30. District fixed effects nearly remove the money effect, member fixed effects remove it entirely, and IV reverses the corporate sign. Spending tracks income: the gubernatorial income elasticity is about 1.1, the stakes (government spending) have no effect, and closeness raises spending. Executives give about 0.05 percent of income, close to the national rate. For Paul's systems the paper is load-bearing. The Melange money engine already cites Ansolabehere to justify cutting MAXSHIFT from 40 to 18 and weighting money below peers. The paper supports that cut on votes. It does not support the access half of the code comment, and it gives no evidence that dollars buy more in competitive seats: closeness raises the supply of money, mostly small individual gifts. On the Mentat side, the consumption account fits the sector growth study's null for industry growth and suggests that donor or national income, not industry revenue, scales giving.

bearings.paper_claim: In the most common House specification (Column 1, 1978-1994, N = 3400, CCUS 0-100 score) an extra 60000 dollars of corporate PAC money (about 1 SD) changes the score by at most 2 points; 50000 dollars of labor PAC money changes it by 6; a change of party changes it by more than 30 points (40 with district FE). Member fixed effects eliminate the contribution effects, and IV reverses the sign on corporate money. Changes in donations to an individual legislator do not translate into changes in that legislator's roll-call votes.
bearings.paper_location: Table 2 and text pp.18-20 (printed NBER pages)
bearings.system_side: shift_lean uses MAXSHIFT times r/(r+HALF) with r = c times amount over receipts. MAXSHIFT defaults to 18 with a code comment citing Ansolabehere for the cut from 40. On median receipts recomputed from congestion.json (1743281, n = 517), a 10k gift shifts lean by about 0.98, below DTHRESH 11.25. Defection needs roughly 1/6 of receipts before the pressure_mult and 1.10 LOSSFRAME factors, which can lower that fraction.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper estimates business-wide PAC money against a Chamber score at ordinary contribution sizes, pooled across the House. The defection channel fires only on scenario shocks near 1/6 of receipts, outside the paper's support. The member-FE null puts the within-member slope at zero, so any nonzero MAXSHIFT is owner judgment, not an estimate. The 2-vs-30 contrast is conditional on party and is not stratified; quote it with an UNSTRATIFIED label.

bearings.paper_claim: Money is a small part of a reelection-minded legislator's calculation: party moves the score by more than 30 points against about 2 for money. The paper lists buying access as one of several group motives and does not test it. It cites 3 billion dollars of lobbying against 300 million of PAC contributions in 1997-98, and Langbein's estimate of about 10000 dollars per legislator hour. Its main thesis is consumption rather than access.
bearings.paper_location: pp.18-20 (votes); pp.31-33 (access, lobbying totals, 20 percent illustration)
bearings.system_side: WM 0.35 and WP 0.65 at flip_model.py:21, with a comment that money buys access and effort more than votes, citing Ansolabehere, Hall and Wayman, and Kalla and Broockman. pflip = a/(a+b) with saturating money terms, each carrying a +1 smoothing term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports money as the minority partner on votes, not on access. The access attribution rests on Kalla and Broockman, which is outside this paper. Peer proximity (cpf_pressure) is not party; the 30-point party effect is only the nearest analogue. With peer terms zero, pflip approaches 0 or 1 only at extreme money ratios because of the +1 smoothing.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims reproduce from text (party 30 vs 2, access untested, 3 billion vs 300 million, Langbein 10000). The WM comment credits Ansolabehere for access, which the paper does not test; this is the citation-precision flag, and it stands. The 0-to-1 range sentence was overstated and is narrowed.

bearings.paper_claim: Closeness raises the quantity of money. In the gubernatorial panel (1976-2000, N = 326, state FE) the closeness coefficient on log per-capita spending is 2.93. In House races of 1992-2000, close seats (under 5 points) draw 60 percent of funds from individuals and 31 percent from PACs, while safe seats (30 points or more) draw 48 and 46 percent. Most of the gap in the individual share comes from gifts under 500 dollars.
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + exp(-max(lean,0)/5) scales effective dollars on both money legs; receipts stay in the denominators of pflip and shift_lean.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows the supply side only: more money, mostly from individuals, flows to close races. It says nothing about per-dollar influence. The PAC evidence is in shares, not dollar levels. Higher receipts in close seats shrink r and partly offset c. Reciprocity is not validated (D-104..D-108), and this paper does not validate it.
bearings.verifier_note: The 2.93 coefficient and the 60/31 and 48/46 splits reproduce. The marginal-dollar wording was wrong: the paper says most of the individual-share gap between close and safe seats comes from gifts under 500 dollars, not that close-race marginal dollars are mostly small gifts. PAC evidence is shares only.

summary_issues: Executive figure: 0.05 percent is a share of annual compensation, not income. The paper says this overstates the income share (p.22). Summary wording should change.

Marginal-dollar wording: the paper says most of the individual-share gap between close and safe seats (60 vs 48) comes from gifts under 500 dollars. It does not say close-race marginal dollars are mostly small gifts.
Defection threshold: the code gives about 0.98 at median receipts (1743281), not 0.9. The 1/6 boundary ignores pressure_mult and LOSSFRAME.
The consumption account 'fits' the sector growth null: the study's own result was not checked in this pass, so the sentence rests only on its config.
Alexander 2009 is described as very large lobbying returns; its text reports positive, significant returns. The contradiction is a framing, not a direct test.
The de Figueiredo 2013 link's stated point (lobbying spending dwarfs PAC giving) was not found in that text.
The summary says the paper supports the MAXSHIFT cut on votes. That holds for the direction, but the paper does not estimate MAXSHIFT, so the cut stays a calibration choice.
gaps_exposed: No component estimates a within-member money-to-position response. MAXSHIFT, HALF, DTHRESH and WM rest on citation, and this paper's member-FE estimate is zero. A check would be a member-FE panel of CU and finance PAC dollars against CU-relevant roll-call or cosponsor alignment, under single-look discipline.

The competitiveness multiplier assumes per-dollar influence rises in close seats, but the only evidence here is that money supply rises (mostly small individual gifts). The effect-heterogeneity question stays untested.

Neither the sector growth study nor the cycle model has a donor-income or national-income scale. The paper finds the spending-to-income ratio flat over 1976-2000, so a ratio-to-income baseline is the natural null.

The system has no consumption or participation channel: every CU dollar is treated as an instrument of influence. Mentat reports employer-matched individual giving as industry giving, which on this paper's account measures participation more than industry strategy.
Access is not modeled separately from votes, although the engine comments say that money buys access.
flags: Citation precision: comments at fec/engine/money_response.py:15 and fec/engine/flip_model.py:21 credit Ansolabehere for the claim that money buys access or effort. This paper lists access as one untested explanation among four or five and argues consumption. Narrow the citation to the claim that money does not buy votes.

The 2-points-vs-30 comparison is a pooled House 1978-1994 coefficient conditional on party controls. Quote it with an UNSTRATIFIED label. The IV and FE estimates change sign and size across specifications.
The 3 billion lobbying vs 300 million PAC figure comes from LDA-era disclosure totals. Under D-021, LDA is an identity source only, so this figure must not justify an LDA-based edge or weight.
The 20 percent return for a subset of PACs (p.32) is an illustration, not an estimate. Do not cite it for an ROI floor.

The extraction notes a garbled Table 2 in which one labor IV cell is starred, against the text's statement that FE effects are insignificant. Cell-level numbers stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
No SNA proposal is argued, so neither rejected proposal (dropping cosponsorship edges, per-edge volume normalization) is in play.
paul_alignment: No Paul annotations (0 entries, 0 annotations). Melange already cites Ansolabehere for its money calibration, and the evidence agrees with MAXSHIFT 18 and WM 0.35 on votes. The paper cuts against Paul's view that money buys access and returns and against his ROI enthusiasm (Alexander 2009): it argues consumption and does not test access. It agrees with the sector growth null, which already undercuts his deep-pockets reading. His competitiveness note (no source says dollars buy more in competitive seats) still holds.

Lobbying ROI analysis under the 2004 American Jobs Creation Act. Its text reports positive, significant lobbying returns, set against this paper's small-return account. The link is a framing contrast, not a direct test. Item exists.
Reports minimal overlap between organizations that lobby and those that make PAC expenditures. It is a check on this paper's claim that big givers also lobby heavily. Item exists.
Studies small individual donors, the consumer contributor this paper puts at the center of campaign finance. Item exists.
Shows ideologically sorted donors, consistent with giving as ideological participation. Item exists.
Fouirnaies and Hall on electoral incentives in U.S. state legislatures. Bears on the competitiveness lever, but for state, not federal, legislators. Item exists.
Links donation timing to lobbying, which complicates a pure consumption reading for organized interests. Item exists.
A co-author's later review of lobbying empirics. The claim that lobbying spending dwarfs PAC giving was not found in its text, so only the agenda link stands. Item exists.
Paul's sector growth source note. The paper's null for stakes and its income elasticity bear on the growth-giving hypothesis. Item exists.

extraction.title: Politics of Feelings: Emotional Expression and Legislative Effectiveness in the U.S. Congress
extraction.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.10198 (v1, 9 Sep 2026); author affiliation University of Konstanz
extraction.document_type: working paper (arXiv preprint, empirical computational social science)
extraction.coverage: Read full text cc88a043bcb2.txt end to end (66,863 chars, 2,232 lines): front matter, abstract, intro, related work, methods, results RQ1-RQ4, discussion, limitations, references, appendices with Tables 1-9. Figures are graphics without images; only captions and printed numbers used. Paul markup: no _annots file for this sha12 (n_annots 0), so paul_markup empty, 0 dropped. Not a Paul note. Metadata hints correct (arXiv 2609.10198, Sep 2026); doi empty (arXiv id only). Brief topics: legislators and text measurement covered; lobbying, networks, allocation, elections not studied.
extraction.research_question: RQ1: how have discrete emotions in U.S. congressional speeches evolved over time, and how do Democrats and Republicans differ? RQ2: how do discrete emotions vary across CAP policy domains? RQ3: how does legislators emotional expression vary with demographic and socio-political characteristics? RQ4: do discrete emotions and broader emotional characteristics (valence, intensity, diversity) explain variation in legislative effectiveness?
extraction.theory: Functional appraisal accounts of emotion (Keltner and Gross 1999); emotions shape attention and persuasion in politics (Marcus 2000); emotion as social information regulating cooperation (Van Kleef 2009); emodiversity and adaptive functioning (Quoidbach et al 2014); stance and appraisal theory (Du Bois 2007; Martin and White 2005). Emotions are treated as communicative resources; the mechanism is not tested.
extraction.data: 1,766,113 Congressional Record floor speeches, 93rd to 118th Congresses (1973 to 2024), House and Senate (Sec 3.1). Duplicates, speeches under 10 words and procedural or presiding-officer speeches removed (zero-shot Llama 3). Unit: speech for emotion scores; legislator-Congress for LES (n = 13,671, Tables 7-9). Trend analysis: 26 Congress-level means per party. Each session at least 20,000 speeches (Fig 5). Topics: 21 CAP major topics, classifier macro F1 0.857 (Sec 3.2.4). LES: Volden and Wiseman, 1973 to 2024.
extraction.method: Transformer multilabel classifier (Widmann and Wich 2023) gives continuous scores for eight emotions per speech, z-standardized over the corpus (Sec 3.2.1). RQ1: Mann-Kendall with Sen slope, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (Table 3). RQ2: CAP topic means and Kruskal-Wallis across 21 topics (Table 4). RQ3: linear mixed-effects per emotion, legislator random intercept, Congress fixed effects, topic controls (Tables 5-6). RQ4: mixed-effects models of member-Congress LES on each emotion or on valence, intensity, diversity (Tables 7-9).
extraction.identification: None stated. The design is associational: the paper estimates whether emotion scores co-vary with LES and does not present an instrument, natural experiment, panel design or sensitivity analysis. Congress fixed effects and topic controls absorb shared time shifts and policy domain only. Reverse direction (effective members changing how they speak) and confounding by leadership or majority status are not separately addressed beyond the included controls.
extraction.scope: U.S. Congress floor speeches, 1973 to 2024 (93rd to 118th). Population: members of the House and Senate who speak on the floor. Not state or supranational legislatures; authors name these as future tests. Measures apply to speech text, not to behavior beyond LES.
extraction.measures: Discrete emotion z-scores (eight). Valence (positive minus negative), intensity (sum), diversity (entropy). Outcome: LES, member-Congress (Volden and Wiseman 2014, 2018). Controls: ideology score (source and direction not stated), party, majority, Senate, female, race, Latino/a, chairs, leadership, first term, seniority, vote share, state experience, speech count and length (log), CAP topic, Congress FE. Validity: AUC on 50 hand-labeled speeches per emotion (Table 1), co-occurrence (Fig 6).
key_findings: RQ1 trends (Sec 4.1, Table 3): Mann-Kendall finds significant increasing trends in mean emotion scores for nearly all emotions in both parties across 26 Congresses. Exception: Democratic joy (tau 0.243, FDR p 0.086). Democratic enthusiasm Sen slope 0.030 per Congress.

Parallel paths (Sec 4.1, Sec 5): Democrats and Republicans follow similar trajectories for most emotions. Authors read the rise as broad intensification of emotional expression, not a shift toward negative rhetoric, since positive and negative emotions both rise.

Anger is volatile (Sec 4.1, Fig 1): Democratic anger peaks in the early 2000s and around 2017; Republican anger is higher in 2021 to 2024. Authors link this volatility to prevailing political context.

Policy domains (RQ2, Sec 4.2, Table 4, Fig 2): Kruskal-Wallis differences significant for all eight emotions across 21 CAP topics, with small effect sizes (epsilon squared 0.013 to 0.034). International Affairs has highest mean fear; Immigration highest mean anger; Education highest pride with elevated joy and enthusiasm; Macroeconomics pairs high anger with low joy and pride.

Demographic and party correlates (RQ3, Sec 4.3, Tables 5-6): female legislators higher enthusiasm (0.020), pride (0.012), joy (0.007), sadness (0.006) and fear (0.004) in standardized units. Senators: lower anger (-0.041) and enthusiasm (-0.007), higher pride (0.009) and joy (0.008). Ideology score: higher anger (0.022), lower joy (-0.004), enthusiasm (-0.002) and pride (-0.006). Marginal R2 ranges 0.003 to 0.071.

Majority party (Tables 5-6): majority members express more joy (0.003), enthusiasm (0.006) and pride (0.009), and less anger (-0.035) and fear (-0.001). Republican coefficients are small, and Republicans express more joy (0.005) and pride (0.005) but less anger (-0.012).

LES, discrete emotions (RQ4, Sec 4.4, Figure 4, Tables 7-8, n = 13,671): enthusiasm 0.016 (95 pct CI 0.007 to 0.025, p under 0.001); pride 0.011 (CI 0.003 to 0.019, p under 0.01); anger -0.037 (CI -0.046 to -0.029, p under 0.001) is the only significant negative. Fear, disgust, sadness, joy and hope are not significant.

Broader characteristics (Sec 4.4, Table 9): emotional diversity 0.026 (CI 0.017 to 0.034) and 0.031 (CI 0.024 to 0.039) across two specifications; valence 0.020 (CI 0.011 to 0.028); intensity -0.014 (CI -0.025 to -0.004, p under 0.01). Marginal R2 is 0.118 to 0.119 in Table 9 versus 0.113 to 0.118 for discrete-emotion models; differences are small.

Classifier validation (Sec 3.2.1, App B, Table 1): in-domain AUC on 50 hand-labeled speeches per emotion (25 highest, 25 lowest scored): anger, joy and hope 1.000; sadness 0.989; enthusiasm 0.982; pride 0.981; fear 0.952; disgust 0.922. No out-of-domain test is reported.

Face validity (Sec 3.2.1, App B, Fig 6, Table 2): top-scoring texts read as plausible exemplars of each emotion (pride as acknowledging colleagues, anger as criticism). Negative emotions correlate weakly and positively with each other; cross-valence correlations are weak.

Corpus scale (Sec 3.1, Fig 5): 1,766,113 speeches; each session at least 20,000; z-standardization preserves each emotion distribution (Sec 3.2.1). Given this N, very small coefficients (0.001 to 0.02 SD) reach p under 0.001, so significance here says little about substantive size.

Interpretation limit (Sec 5): authors call emotions consequential and say expression shapes persuasion, coordination and relationships, but no mechanism, causes or targets of emotion are tested; authors list identifying causes and targets as future work.
limitations: Stated by authors (Sec 5 Limitations): findings are for the U.S. Congress only; generalization to state legislatures or the European Parliament is open.
Stated by authors: causes and targets of emotional expression are not identified; CAP topics are the only context control.
Stated by authors: the eight emotions are a selective set; curiosity, guilt, shame and nostalgia are not examined.

summary_md: Aroyehun (arXiv 2609.10198, Sep 2026) scores 1,766,113 Congressional Record floor speeches (93rd-118th Congresses, 1973-2024) for eight discrete emotions with a transformer multilabel classifier (Widmann and Wich 2023), z-standardized over the corpus. Four questions: trends (Mann-Kendall over 26 Congress means: nearly every emotion rises in both parties, read as intensification rather than a negative turn), policy domains (all eight differ across 21 CAP topics, but epsilon squared only 0.013-0.034), member correlates (mixed models: majority members show less anger, -0.035; senators less anger, -0.041; women more enthusiasm, +0.020; ideology score more anger, +0.022; marginal R2 0.003-0.071), and legislative effectiveness. On the Volden-Wiseman LES (member-Congress, n = 13,671), enthusiasm (+0.016) and pride (+0.011) are positive, anger (-0.037) is the only negative, and emotional diversity (+0.026 to +0.031) and valence (+0.020) beat intensity (-0.014). Marginal R2 moves only from about 0.113 to 0.119, so emotion adds little beyond the controls. The design is associational: no identification strategy, reverse causation is not addressed, validation is 50 extreme-scored speeches per emotion in-domain only, the classifier was built on German political text, and the paper has internal inconsistencies (random intercepts vs fixed effects, table labels). For Paul's systems it matters in three places. It uses the same CEL LES that fec/members/lep_criterion.py pulls as an external criterion. It shows speech-emotion features vary with chamber, majority status and gender, which the affective-N slot controls only partly. And its valence vs intensity split matches the two LSD fields already computed in Draft Systems. Nothing here justifies adding an emotion feature to rank. All coefficients are UNVERIFIED in this project (DE-062).

extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (about 94.5k chars, 3118 lines) in chunks: front matter, abstract, introduction, theory (Sec 2), data (Sec 3), results (Sec 4), extensions (Sec 5: heterogeneity, parties, timing, robustness), conclusion, references and all tables 1 to 8 plus Table A.1. Extraction garbles Greek symbols (phi, xi, eta, theta) and some table columns are ambiguous; figures (Figure 1 network plot) read from caption only. Metadata hints checked: title, authors, year 2018 and NBER WP 24442 are correct; kind hint academic-article corrected to working paper; no DOI in text so left blank.
extraction.research_question: Do social connections (cosponsorship ties among members of Congress) causally raise legislative effectiveness, once the endogeneity of those ties is controlled, and does the network effect predicted by the model beat traditional centrality measures?
extraction.data: Legislative Effectiveness Scores (LES) for U.S. House members from Volden and Wiseman (2014), 109th to 113th Congresses (election cycles 2004 to 2012). Unit: member-congress; N = 2,176 connected congressmen (about 433 Representatives per Congress, including midterm replacements). Cosponsorship network built from THOMAS: two members linked if they cosponsored the same bill, weights = shared bills over total bills cosponsored. Instrument network: alumni ties from the Biographical Directory of Congress, two members linked if they attended the same institution within an 8-year window; about 40 percent of members linked. First-stage dyadic sample: 945,382 dyads (Table 1). Controls: seniority, margin of victory, DW-NOMINATE distance to median, size of state delegation, gender, race, party, committee chair, majority and minority leader, Speaker, Congress fixed effects.
extraction.method: Structural model yields equilibrium effectiveness E = [I - phi W]^-1 (beta x + epsilon) style spatial autoregressive system (eqs 5-7). Estimated by nonlinear least squares (NLLS). Endogeneity handled by a two-step Heckman-type control function: first stage dyadic OLS of cosponsorship links on alumni links, covariates and absolute differences; selection term xi built from first-stage residuals and inserted in the outcome equation (eqs 8-10). Standard errors from residual bootstrap with 500 replications resampling structural errors by Congress. Partial F tests for phi = 0. Robustness: committee fixed effects (21 committees), state legislative experience subsample, heterogeneous spillovers (eqs 11-14), within- versus between-party networks (eqs 15-17), outcome split by legislative stage (Table 7).
extraction.scope: U.S. House of Representatives only (the Senate is discussed but not analyzed), 109th to 113th Congresses (2004 to 2012 election cycles). The sample covers members with cosponsorship and alumni data, so 2,176 member-congress observations rather than all members. Results are for LES as defined by Volden and Wiseman.
key_findings: Theory (Sec 2.2, Proposition 1): unique Nash equilibrium in which effectiveness equals a weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the social network, given Assumption 1 (invertibility). With no spillovers the model reduces to the standard characteristics-only model.
Uncorrected NLLS (Table 2, col 2): network spillover phi = 0.4448 (SE 0.0233); partial F test of phi = 0 gives 350.81, reported p below 0.001. Positive and significant, consistent with externalities.

Corrected NLLS (Table 2, col 3, bootstrap SE): phi = 0.8324 (SE 0.0516); selection term xi = -0.4133 (SE 0.0741), significant; partial F = 59.51. Phi rises and stays significant after correction, which the authors read as network endogeneity biasing naive estimates downward for phi and biasing characteristic effects upward.

Committee chair effect (Table 2, Sec 4, p.16-17): OLS 1.9669 (SE 0.1147) versus 1.6107 (SE 0.1545) in the corrected network model, about 18 percent smaller in magnitude. The authors say OLS partly captures network effects.

Traditional centralities (Table 4): OLS betweenness 0.0079, closeness 0.0011 and eigenvector 0.1203 are all significant, but after the correction none is significant (betweenness -0.2599 SE 0.1662; closeness 0.0085 SE 0.0086; eigenvector -0.4122 SE 0.2500).

Horse race (Table 4, last block): when the model term is included with the other centralities, only phi stays significant; reported Phi = 0.7095 (SE 0.0817). Text cites this as Column (8) but the table header lists seven columns, so the column mapping is uncertain.

First stage (Table 1, 945,382 dyads): alumni-tie coefficient 3.8658 (SE 0.194) with full controls, stated as multiplied by hundreds; R-squared rises from 0.0007 (alumni only) to about 0.079 with controls, supporting alumni ties as a predictor of cosponsorship links.

Heterogeneous spillovers (Tables 5a and 5b, as parsed): the susceptibility coefficient for No White is 0.1584 (SE 0.0955, significant at 10 percent); seniority is -0.0339 (SE 0.0123); the committee-chair cell is -0.5981 (SE 0.1588). Text: minorities gain more, senior members and chairs gain less.

Party ties (Table 6): the between-party term is 0.8668 (SE 0.2136) and the within-party term 0.8346 (SE 0.0584) in the last column; the first column has 1.5984 (SE 0.4742) vs 1.4208 (SE 0.1000). The gap is small relative to SEs in the corrected columns, so the claim that cross-party ties matter more is only weakly supported in these numbers.

Legislative stage (Table 7, corrected Phi): BILL only 0.5634 (SE 0.0539); BILL plus AIC 0.8387 (SE 0.0465); ABC plus PASS plus LAW 0.8643 (SE 0.0767). Network effects are positive and significant at all stages and larger later; xi is significant in each corrected column.

Robustness (Table 8): with committee fixed effects, corrected Phi = 0.7114 (SE 0.0664) on N = 2,176; on the state-experience subsample (N = 1,775) corrected Phi = 0.8150 (SE 0.0517). Estimates are stable; table column labels conflict with the text on which columns carry committee dummies.
limitations: Working paper, not peer-reviewed (NBER disclaimer, p.1).

Identification relies on the alumni network being exogenous to politics and relevant for cosponsorship; the paper asserts this and gives no formal exclusion test. Footnote 5 notes identification may also come from nonlinearities alone.
Selection term xi is a generated regressor; bootstrap resamples structural errors only, and the authors note no closed-form NLLS standard errors exist in this network setting.
Alumni links cover only about 40 percent of members, so the sample is 2,176 member-congress observations, not the full chamber.
Assumption 1 (invertibility, positivity) is assumed for the empirical range, not verified; the authors say it fails only with very large spillovers.
Model and results are for House LES only; the Senate is not analyzed and LES is a single composite index with weights set by Volden and Wiseman.
Text calls the correction Heckman but the procedure is a two-step control function, as the paper's own footnote 4 notes (citing Qu and Lee 2015).
Table and text references conflict: horse-race column (8) vs seven headed columns; committee dummies placed in Table 8 columns 5-6 in the table but in columns 1-2 in the text.

extraction.theory: Each legislator chooses effort to maximize his own effectiveness, which depends on his characteristics, his effort, and the effectiveness of socially connected colleagues weighted by tie strength (complementarity between own effort and peers' effectiveness). Simultaneous effort choice gives a linear equilibrium in which effectiveness is a weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality (Ballester, Calvo-Armengol and Zenou 2006 style) with weights set by member characteristics. The paper says the equilibrium is unique under Assumption 1 and that the model nests the standard characteristics-only regression at phi = 0.
extraction.identification: Two-step control function (Heckman-type) for an endogenous network. Stage 1: dyadic link-formation regression of cosponsorship ties on alumni ties, dyad-level differences in characteristics (absolute values), and covariates. Stage 2: NLLS of the spatial model with xi, the function of stage-1 residuals, added to the outcome equation; joint normality (Assumption 2) implies a common selection effect across members. Exclusion restriction: alumni ties affect LES only through cosponsorship. Footnote 5 says identification could come from nonlinearity without exclusion restrictions.
extraction.measures: Outcome: Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES), weighted average of BILL, AIC, ABC, PASS and LAW indicators normalized to mean 1 per Congress (mean 1.0081, SD 1.47 in Table A.1). Network: cosponsorship share and alumni share (institutions shared within 8 years over institutions attended). Centralities: Bonacich (model), betweenness, closeness, eigenvector. Controls: seniority, margin of victory (vote share), DW-NOMINATE absolute first dimension (distance to median), delegation size, party, gender, race (No White), committee chair, majority and minority leader, Speaker.

summary_md: Battaglini, Leone Sciabolazza and Patacchini (NBER WP 24442, 2018; a working paper, not peer reviewed) model House members who put effort into lawmaking and gain from the effectiveness of the colleagues they cosponsor with. In equilibrium, a member's Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES) is proportional to a characteristic-weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the cosponsorship network. They estimate this by nonlinear least squares on 2,176 member-Congress observations (House, 109th to 113th Congresses). Cosponsorship ties are endogenous, so they correct with a two-step control function that uses shared-alma-mater ties as the instrument (first stage on 945,382 dyads). The spillover parameter phi is 0.44 uncorrected and 0.83 corrected (SE 0.05). The selection term is significant. Betweenness, closeness and eigenvector centrality are each significant in naive OLS, but none is significant after the correction. In a horse race, only the model-derived Katz-Bonacich term survives (phi 0.71). The committee-chair effect shrinks about 18 percent (1.97 to 1.61) once the network enters the model. Network effects are positive at every stage from BILL to LAW and grow at later stages. Cross-party and within-party ties have similar coefficients (0.87 vs 0.83), and the gap is small next to their standard errors. For Paul's systems, the paper is the empirical twin of the 2016 targeting paper behind the diagnostic Katz-Bonacich benchmark. It supports the June decision to retire the direction-blind InfluenceScore blend. It also flags that the live cosponsor graph is used without any endogeneity correction. The system already loads CEL LES data, so a direct replication of this paper's KB-to-LES link is cheap. That replication has not been run, and any such result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

extraction.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (50,533 chars, 890 lines of extracted text, printed pages 1-26). No ext/rel override files existed. Read: front matter, abstract, intro (1-2), NLI framing (3-4), PolNLI dataset incl. Table 1 (4-8), training (8), zero-shot results (9-11), few-shot results (12-14), timing (14-15), limitations and model use (15-17), conclusion (17-18), references, Appendices A-C (19-26). Paul markup: none. annot_sha12s is empty and no _annots/3859f20b633a.json exists. Page images not rendered; locations are printed page numbers. Metadata hints checked: title, four authors, year 2024 and preprint status are correct; venue arXiv; no DOI in text. Topic check: the paper has no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation, election, persuasion or turnout content. Legislators appear only as stance targets in the PolNLI sources (Polistance datasets, p.23). Text measurement is the whole paper. Reader observation, not an authors claim: GPT-4o relabeling and filtering (p.6-7) and GPT-4o hypothesis augmentation (p.7) mean the PolNLI labels share an LLM source; the authors exclude GPT-4o from the benchmark for that reason (p.10). Figure values (Figs 1-5) are not in the text, so per-model MCC and timing figures are not extracted.
extraction.research_question: Can small, domain-adapted natural language inference (NLI) encoder models trained on political text match or beat zero-shot large language models and supervised classifiers for political text classification, and can they be few-shot trained from 10-25 labeled documents, while staying open and efficient? (p.1-2)
extraction.theory: No formal theory. Argument: NLI framing turns any classification into a document-hypothesis entailment task, and narrowing a small pretrained encoder to one domain reduces the model size needed for high performance; transfer from general NLI models speeds adaptation (p.2-4, p.8).
extraction.data: PolNLI: 201,691 political documents, 852 unique entailment hypotheses, 22 datasets in four tasks: stance 11 datasets, 361 hypotheses, 66,581 documents; topic 5, 278, 62,005; hate-speech/toxicity 2, 177, 41,871; event extraction 4, 36, 31,234 (Table 1, p.5). Sources include tweets, news, congressional newsletters, legislation, party platforms, State of the Union speeches, Supreme Court case summaries, ACLED and SCAD event records, and crowd-sourced arguments (Appendix A, p.23). Unit: document paired with a hypothesis, labeled entail or not entail. After augmentation there are 2,834 unique entailment phrasings (p.7). Split: test and validation sets of about 15,000 documents each, split by hypothesis so test hypotheses are unseen in training; validation is about 10,000 unseen-hypothesis and 5,000 seen-hypothesis documents (p.7-8). Few-shot test cases: Mood of the Nation open-text democracy answers (liberty and rights) and COVID-19 threat-minimization tweets, about 2,000 tweets in Block Jr. et al. (p.12-14). Timing: 5,000 PolNLI test documents (p.14).
extraction.method: Fine-tunes DeBERTa V3 base (86M parameters) and large (304M) models that were already trained for general NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), using the Transformers library (p.2, p.8). Label cleaning removes source metadata; hypotheses are written per label (p.5-6). Labels are validated by GPT-4o; documents where human and LLM labels disagree are dropped (p.6-7). Hypotheses are augmented with GPT-4o synonyms and manual review (p.7). Checkpoints chosen by training loss, validation loss, MCC, F1, accuracy and per-task consistency, plus qualitative tests with punctuation, capitalization and wording edits (p.8). Zero-shot benchmark against DeBERTa base and large NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; GPT-4o not benchmarked (p.9). Few-shot: simple random samples of 10, 25, 50 and 100 documents, 10 repetitions each, 95% confidence intervals, default learning rate, 5 epochs, no hyperparameter or hypothesis search (p.12). Timing: same 5,000 documents with hypothesis 'This text is about politics' on RTX 3090, Tesla T4, M3 Max and Ryzen 9 5900x (p.14).
extraction.identification: Not causal. Generalization is judged by splitting test documents on unseen hypotheses (p.7-8) and by few-shot learning curves at sample sizes 10, 25, 50 and 100 (p.12).
extraction.measures: Primary metric: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), chosen for robustness on binary tasks (p.9). Also accuracy and F1 (checkpoint selection, p.8; COVID accuracy, p.14; Llama accuracy, p.13). Bootstrapped standard errors for Fig. 1 (p.9-10); 95% confidence intervals across 10 few-shot repetitions (p.12). Timing: documents per second by hardware (Fig. 5, p.15; values not in text).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language political text from social media, news, newsletters, legislation, party platforms, speeches, court summaries, event reports and crowd-sourced arguments (Appendix A, p.23). Language: English only (p.17). Era: sources span several years; references were accessed in June 2024 (p.19-22). Tasks: stance, topic, hate-speech and toxicity, and event classification (p.4).
key_findings: PolNLI test set, all tasks combined: DEBATE models are more performative than DeBERTa base and large NLI, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet in zero-shot MCC; per-model values appear only in Fig. 1 (p.9-10).
Stance: DEBATE models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are significantly better than the other models on stance detection; event extraction is comparable between DEBATE and the two LLMs (p.9).
Hate-speech: DEBATE models are significantly better than the other models; the authors attribute this to subjective definitions that the models were tuned to (p.9-10).
Polistance Quote Tweets (stance, hardest set): Claude 3.5 MCC 0.29; DEBATE base MCC 0.62 and large MCC 0.88; DeBERTa Large had negative correlation with the correct label on this dataset (p.10).

Few-shot, Mood of the Nation liberty and rights: Llama 3.1 is best zero-shot (reported MCC 0.74, accuracy 88%); after 10 samples both DEBATE models jump and do not differ significantly from Llama; at 25 the large model significantly beats Llama; at 50 the base model matches it (p.13).

Few-shot, COVID-19 threat minimization: base model largely fails zero-shot and does not match the supervised Electra classifier (MCC 0.66 on 2,000 tweets) at 100 samples; large model matches it at 10 samples (MCC 0.67, accuracy 87%) and exceeds it at 25 (MCC 0.69, accuracy 88%) (p.13-14).

Efficiency: DEBATE models give large speed advantages over Llama 3.1 8B on all four tested hardware types; a laptop GPU (M3 Max) or free cloud GPU (Tesla T4) classifies documents at a brisk pace; exact timings are in Fig. 5 only (p.14-15).
Training: base model learning rate 2e-5, batch 8, 20 epochs; large model learning rate 9e-6, batch 4 with gradient accumulation 4, 20 epochs; checkpoint per epoch (Appendix C, p.25-26).
Recommendation: use the large model for zero-shot and most few-shot work; the base model for simple few-shot or supervised work (p.15-16).
Recommendation: keep NLI hypotheses short and template-like; use few-shot training when a task needs long hypotheses with several conditions, or is far from the PolNLI sources (p.16-17).
Stated limitation with a finding: the authors do not expect DEBATE to beat proprietary LLMs on all tasks; LLMs are expected to generalize better to tasks far from PolNLI (p.17).
Validation: GPT-4o labels matched manual review on 92.5% of 400 sampled documents (Cohen's kappa 0.85); 14 of 400 (3.5%) were judged wrong LLM labels (p.7).
limitations: Trained and evaluated only on English documents; performance on other languages is unknown (p.17).
Not expected to outperform proprietary LLMs on every task; LLMs expected to generalize better to tasks far from PolNLI (p.17).
NLI hypotheses must be short; no clear measure of task simplicity exists, only qualitative judgments (p.16).
Labels for topic and event data were positive-only; negatives were created by random reassignment, and multi-topic documents are a known concern addressed only by validation (p.6-7).
Authors discourage benchmarking OpenAI models on PolNLI because GPT-4o was used in label validation (p.10).
Few-shot runs used no hyperparameter or hypothesis search, by design, so the results are not tuned (p.12).
short_quotes: A simple random sample of only 10-25 labeled documents is sufficient to teach the models complex labeling tasks when necessary.
Because of this, it is little wonder that LLMs have received widespread adoption within political and other social sciences.

summary_md: Burnham, Kahn, Wang and Peng (arXiv 2024) release Political DEBATE: DeBERTa V3 base (86M) and large (304M) NLI classifiers, further trained on PolNLI. PolNLI holds 201,691 political documents and 852 hypotheses across stance, topic, hate-speech and event tasks, and its sources include congressional newsletters. On test hypotheses unseen in training, both models beat general NLI models, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on zero-shot MCC. On the hardest stance set (quote tweets), Claude scores MCC 0.29, base 0.62 and large 0.88. In few-shot training, 10 to 25 random labeled documents are often enough. The base model, however, failed the bespoke COVID threat-minimization task and could not match a supervised classifier (MCC 0.66) even at 100 samples, while the large model matched it at 10 (0.67). The authors therefore recommend the large model whenever feasible, short single-condition hypotheses, and supervised training when labels need meta-knowledge or a bespoke concept. The labels were validated with GPT-4o, so GPT-4o is excluded from the benchmark. For Paul, this is the actual checkpoint behind the Melange CU press stance reader. The system fine-tunes the base model on 552 labeled releases. Its own history follows the paper's pattern: base zero-shot reached 53% accuracy with oppose F1 0.08, and fine-tuning raised it to 87% agreement with Claude. Its valence-hop bottleneck matches the paper's warning about bespoke concepts. The bearings are on the model choice (base, not large), hypothesis design (a compound neutral hypothesis), the evaluation metric (accuracy and kappa against an LLM reference rather than MCC against humans), and the planned ACU speaker-mode branching. Nothing here touches the SNA or LDA rules.

bearings.paper_claim: Political DEBATE base and large are DeBERTa V3 NLI models (starting from Laurer et al. 2023 NLI checkpoints) further trained on PolNLI, 201,691 documents and 852 hypotheses. Each document is paired with a templated hypothesis and labeled entail or not entail. Full-training base hyperparameters: learning rate 2e-5 for 20 epochs (Appendix C.1). Few-shot runs used the default learning rate for 5 epochs with no tuning.

extraction.research_question: How should difference-in-differences designs with a continuous or multi-valued dose be identified, interpreted and estimated? Which causal parameters are identified under standard parallel trends versus stronger assumptions, and what does the common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression with a dose-by-post interaction actually estimate?
extraction.theory: Potential outcomes indexed by dose (Robins 1986). Distinguishes level treatment effects Y(d)-Y(0) from causal responses, the marginal derivative in dose (Angrist and Imbens 1995). Generalizes Fricke (2017) from two doses to continuous and multi-valued doses. Uses Yitzhaki (1996) linear-projection decomposition of regression slopes. The empirical interpretation of the derivative as an elasticity of substitution comes from a homothetic two-factor hospital production model following Acemoglu and Finkelstein (2008).
extraction.data: Application: Acemoglu and Finkelstein (2008) AHA Annual Survey Database hospital panel. Balanced panel of 5881 hospitals; pre period averaged over 1980-1983 and post period over 1984-1986 (Sec 6, p.25). Dose M is the 1983 Medicare inpatient share; among treated hospitals mean 0.45, SD 0.15 (Sec 2, p.5). 4987 hospitals have a positive dose; 57 above 0.75, 20 above 0.80, 3 above 0.90 (Sec 6.2, p.28). Outcome is the depreciation share of total operating expenses as a capital-labor proxy; 1983 mean 4.5; untreated mean change 0.37 (Fig 4 note, p.27). Figure 1 uses 1980-1986 annual data and drops 860 of 6741 hospitals with missing outcomes. Policy: 1983 PPS set the labor subsidy to zero and left the capital subsidy unchanged.
extraction.method: Two-period DiD with continuous dose, identified under parallel trends (PT, Assumption PT) and strong parallel trends (SPT, Assumption SPT). Estimators: (i) binarized DiD regression of the outcome change on an indicator for positive dose (eq 4.6), which recovers ATT_glob under SPT; (ii) saturated regression with dose dummies for discrete doses (eq 4.1); (iii) quadratic parametric regression among treated units (eq 4.2); (iv) nonparametric sieve regression with cubic B-splines and a data-driven Lepski-type sieve dimension (Chen, Christensen and Kankanala 2025), with honest uniform confidence bands (Appendix B). ACRT_glob is the sample mean of estimated ACRT(D_i) over treated units. TWFE is decomposed (Theorem 3.4) into causal response, levels, scaled levels and scaled 2x2 representations with explicit weights (Table 1). Extensions: staggered timing (Appendix C), relaxing SPT through bounds, sub-regions and covariate-conditional SPT (Sec 5). Pre-trend checks use event-study versions ATT_loc(e) and ACRT_loc(e). Inference clusters at the hospital level.
extraction.identification: Under PT, ATT(d|d) = E[dY|D=d] - E[dY|D=0] and ATT_loc = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] are identified, but comparisons across dose groups mix causal responses with selection bias (Thm 3.1, 3.2). Under SPT, ATT(d) and ACRT(d) are identified, and ATT_glob = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] and ACRT_glob = E of the dose-density-weighted derivative of E[dY|D=d] (Thm 3.3, Cor 3.1). Without untreated units, the dose-group comparison to the lowest dose recovers differences only, and interpreting them causally requires strengthening PT (Remark 3.1). Pre-period data cannot test SPT (p.13-14).
extraction.measures: Outcome: depreciation share of total operating expenses (capital-labor ratio proxy). Dose: 1983 Medicare inpatient share M. Causal parameters: ATT(d|d), ATT(d), ACRT(d|d), ACRT(d), ATT_loc, ATT_glob, ACRT_loc, ACRT_glob, event-study ATT_loc(e) and ACRT_loc(e). TWFE coefficient beta_twfe from Equation 1.1 with hospital and year fixed effects.
extraction.scope: Population: US hospitals in the Acemoglu and Finkelstein balanced panel subject to the 1983 Medicare PPS labor-subsidy change. Era: 1980-1986. The identification and estimation results apply to any two-period DiD with a continuous or multi-valued dose, and to staggered designs in Appendix C. The empirical content is a single application, not a general estimate.
key_findings: Under PT, ATT(d|d) and ATT_loc = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] are identified (Thm 3.1, p.10). The main text makes clear that ATT(d) is not identified under PT alone.
Under PT alone, comparing outcome paths across dose groups mixes a causal response with a selection bias term ATT(l|h) - ATT(l|l); causal responses are not identified (Thm 3.2, p.11).
Under SPT, ATT(d), ACRT(d), ATT_glob and ACRT_glob are identified; ACRT_glob equals the average derivative weighted by the dose density among treated (Thm 3.3, Cor 3.1, p.12-14).
The TWFE coefficient is a weighted integral of ATT(d|d) whose weights integrate to zero, with negative weights below the mean dose and positive above (Thm 3.4(b), p.16-17).

Under PT, the TWFE causal-response decomposition is a convex average of ACRT(d|d) plus selection bias, with positive weights integrating to one (Thm 3.4(a), p.16). Positive weights do not make TWFE a natural target.
Equation 3.1 writes beta_twfe as a Wald-type ratio with distance weights; in the application the numerator is 0.60 and the denominator 0.53 (p.17, p.28).
Nonparametric ATT_loc = 0.80 (s.e. 0.05), about 18 percent of the 1983 mean outcome of 4.5; reject zero for doses 0.05 to 0.78, covering 96 percent of treated hospitals (Sec 6.2, p.27).

Static TWFE coefficient is 1.14 (s.e. 0.099, Fig 1); it is close to ATT_loc only because two biases offset. Dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent while causal responses are unchanged (p.3, p.28, p.30).
ACRT_glob = -0.08 (s.e. 0.19), not significantly different from zero; estimated ACRT(m) is negative for m above 0.41, covering 71 percent of treated hospitals (Sec 6.3, p.30).
Post-period average of the ATT event study is 0.755 (s.e. 0.048) (Fig 8, p.30); post-period average of the ACRT event study is 0.220 (s.e. 0.170) (Fig 10, p.32).
Pre-treatment ACRT event-study estimates reject the zero implied by no-anticipation plus parallel trends in 1981, though the violation is small relative to post-period effects (p.32).

Implied average elasticity of substitution point estimates do not fit the positive-elasticity prediction, although the uniform bands do not reject zero; the authors treat this as evidence against SPT or the two-factor model (p.31-32).
limitations: SPT is described as strong and perhaps implausible in many applications; the authors do not propose it as a default (p.13).
Pre-trend tests cannot distinguish PT from SPT, because pre-period outcomes are untreated potential outcomes (p.13-14).

Event-study pre-trend tests may miss PT violations; aggregate PT allows violations that average to zero across dose groups, and whether that should count as evidence against the design is debated (p.24-25).

Quadratic parametric estimates are precise only if the functional form is correct; pretesting parametric against nonparametric fits can mislead, so the authors use honest nonparametric bands (p.28-29).
Nonparametric precision is limited where doses are sparse, with only 57 treated hospitals above dose 0.75 (p.28).
Footnote 12: the sieve dimension used for ACRT_glob is treated as non-random; the randomness of the Lepski-type selection is left for future research (p.30).
A Neyman-orthogonal representation for ACRT_glob suggests double machine learning, which the paper leaves for future research (p.22).
Without untreated units, ATT(d|d) and the levels decompositions are not identified; only dose-group differences are identified (Remark 3.1, Remark 3.2, p.14-15).
The 1983 pre-PPS event-study coefficient may reflect partial 1983 PPS effects and fiscal-year reporting (footnote 11, p.29).

The elasticity interpretation assumes no anticipation and a homothetic two-factor production model; the authors note alternatives such as a three-factor or non-homothetic model could rationalize the negative ACRT (p.31-32).

Formal estimation for the staggered case is not provided; the authors say disaggregated results apply directly and that binarized event-study procedures can be used when ATT_loc(e) is the target (Remark C.1, p.42).
TWFE beta depends on the unit of dose: recoding the dose from 0 to 100 shrinks beta from 1.14 to 0.0114 while ATT_loc is unchanged (p.28).
short_quotes: Strong parallel trends may not be plausible in many applications.
comparing these parameters across treatments is challenging because parallel trends does not rule out selection bias.
a researcher confusing a small ACRT for an ATT would mistakenly conclude that a policy was ineffective.

summary_md: Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (arXiv 2107.02637v8, 2025) work out what difference-in-differences identifies when treatment comes as a continuous dose rather than an on/off switch. Under ordinary parallel trends, only effects for the units that actually got dose d are identified (ATT(d|d), and ATT_loc pooled over treated units). Comparing outcomes across dose levels mixes the causal response with a selection-bias term (Thm 3.2). Causal responses such as ACRT(d), the derivative in dose, need strong parallel trends: the response to each dose must be the same across dose groups. Pre-period data cannot test that assumption. The common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) dose-by-post slope is a weighted average with non-obvious weights. In the levels form those weights integrate to zero and are negative below the mean dose (Thm 3.4). The slope also depends on the dose units and on whether untreated units are included. In the Medicare PPS hospital application (5,881 hospitals, 1980-1986), TWFE gives 1.14. That sits near ATT_loc = 0.80 only because two biases offset. ACRT_glob = -0.08 (s.e. 0.19), and dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent while the causal responses do not move. Estimation uses binarized DiD plus B-spline sieve regressions with honest uniform bands. The paper bears most on the Mentat sector-growth regressions, which put a continuous growth measure into sector-plus-year fixed-effects models with no zero-dose group. It also bears, as a design template, on the open question of whether money's effect is concave, which the Melange money terms assume but never estimate. Purely econometric. No lobbying, network or legislator content.

summary_issues: The summary says the Mentat growth regressions use sector-plus-year fixed effects. Year FE appear only in the robustness variants R-yearFE and R-logFE (sgs_registry.R:664-671); the primary specifications were not fully traced here.

All other summary numbers check against the text: 5881 hospitals, 1980-1986, TWFE 1.14, ATT_loc 0.80, ACRT_glob -0.08, 78 percent shrinkage, 0.0114 recoding, and the Thm 3.4b sign pattern. Purely econometric scope is correct, with no lobbying, network or legislator content.
gaps_exposed: No estimated money dose-response anywhere: the saturating shapes in flip_model.py and money_response.py are priors, not fitted from a before/after panel with an unfunded comparison group.

Sector-growth fits report a pooled growth slope but not the implicit weights each sector-year gets (the Eq 3.1 Wald-type numerator and denominator). So a null cannot be told apart from offsetting heterogeneous sector responses.
Sector growth has no zero-dose group. Under the paper's Remark 3.1, any growth contrast is identified only relative to other growth levels, not relative to no growth.
Growth is non-absorbing and time-varying. The study has no estimator built for switching continuous treatments (e.g. de Chaisemartin-D'Haultfoeuille style), only TWFE and first-difference variants.
flags: No conflict with brain rules. The sector-growth code already labels year-FE pooled slopes UNSTRATIFIED (sgs_estimate.R:250-256) and frames results as associations only (sgs_report.R:593), as the pooled-coefficient rule requires.
The paper's application is hospitals under Medicare PPS, not political spending. Any transfer to giving or legislator behaviour is a design lesson, not an effect size.
No Paul annotations exist for this work (annot_sha12s empty; paul_entries empty), so there is no stated takeaway to check against.
paul_alignment: Paul has no entry or markup for this paper, so there is no takeaway to compare. His sector-growth position cites the Imai and Kim two-way fixed effects caution. This paper extends that caution from binary to continuous treatment and agrees with it: TWFE slopes on a dose are weighted mixtures that need strong parallel trends for a causal-response reading. The system already treats these slopes as non-causal associations and reports a null growth effect. No current note is made stale; the paper gives a sharper reason not to read the null as no effect.

related.why: Imai and Kim (Political Analysis 2021) critique two-way fixed effects with panel treatments; this paper gives the continuous-dose analogue of that caution. Item exists and is linked to the same sector-growth component.
